title: CSV Coordinate Validator: Catch Bad Rows First
description: Validate a coordinate CSV before mapping with the CSV Coordinate Validator — missing columns, non-numeric values and out-of-range pairs caught. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a CRM export with one latitude of 140.7 and two blank longitudes fails here in seconds — instead of failing silently on the customer’s map an hour later.
quick_answer: The CSV Coordinate Validator checks a coordinate CSV before you map it, catching missing coordinate columns, non-numeric values and latitude/longitude pairs outside WGS84 ranges. Paste the file and read the row-level verdicts — the QA step that keeps bad rows off your map.

body.t: Business data was never born geospatial. The validator finds the rows where an address, a note or a stray comma moved into the coordinate columns. Clean files then flow to the
Spatial databases reject or — worse — misplace bad rows. Gate the import here and the database stays trustworthy.
A purchased list’s quality is measurable: the share of invalid rows is the number the refund conversation needs.
Rows that already carry valid coordinates should skip geocoding entirely. Validation separates the done from the to-do before credits burn.

Latitude 140.7 (a longitude in the wrong column), longitude ‘N/A’ (a note in a number’s chair), and an empty pair (a row that never had coordinates). Every bad file you will ever meet is variations on these three.

popular_table.note: Validation is about form, not truth: a row can be valid and still be the wrong place. Provenance is checked against sources; form is checked here, completely.

faq: Common latitude/longitude spellings (lat, latitude, y and lon, lng, longitude, x among them). Exotic headers can be renamed in the pasted snippet — the snippet is a copy, your file stays untouched.
Does it fix the bad rows?
It names them and their failure. Fixes belong in your editor, where the row’s story is visible — a tool that silently ‘repairs’ coordinates invents geography.
Six-digit eastings fail the degree ranges loudly — that failure is the diagnosis. Convert projected data with GIS before validating here.
Valid in form, famous in practice: 0,0 in the Gulf of Guinea collects every defaulted and un-geocoded row in history. The validator passes them; your eyebrow should not.
‘40°45′N’ is text to a CSV parser. Convert to decimals first (the DMS converters here), then validate the numeric file.
Semicolon files parse as one wide column and the coordinate columns go missing — the validator’s first check reports exactly that, which is the fix’s signpost.
How many rows can I paste?
Paste-sized files run instantly in the browser. Million-row pipelines belong to scripts — with this page defining the rules they should implement.
